title: Few supports for life
hookLine: every pill bottle lists side effects; Nagarjuna says even the few supports of life can turn against it
tomorrow: at the very end, what actually helps?

lines: WHAT KEEPS YOU ALIVE CAN HURT.
cards: Every pill bottle comes with a folded sheet of side effects in tiny print. Food has its own warnings: allergies, choking hazards, best before. So can the very things that keep you alive also hurt you?
Nagarjuna said yes, plainly, in a second letter of advice to a king, and Buddhists have leaned different ways on what to do with it.

teach.b: In his Precious Garland, Nagarjuna writes that the causes of death are many, the things that keep us alive are few, and even those can become causes of death. Food, medicine, shelter, warmth: the few supports.
And the same food can choke; the same medicine can harm. So what do you do with a body like that? Buddhists have leaned two ways, and both have deep roots.
The first view: care for it.

In the traditional story of the Buddha's life, he nearly starved himself in harsh practice, then accepted a bowl of milk-rice from a young woman named Sujata, and with his strength back, sat down and woke up.
The body is the boat you cross in; neglect it and there's no crossing.
The second view: don't cling to it. The few supports will fail sooner or later, and if all your peace hangs on them, there's no peace. Hold the body like something borrowed.
Here's a place the two meet.

teach.h: USE IT WISELY, FOR THE PRACTICE.
teach.b: In the Majjhima Nikaya, monks learn a reflection for every meal and every medicine: I use this wisely, not for fun or for show, but to keep this body going, to ease pain and sickness, so the practice can go on.
Care, fully. Cling, not at all.
Few supports: tend them well, and don't lean your whole weight on them.

how: In Theravada monasteries monks and nuns recite reflections on the use of food, robes, lodging and medicine, often daily; lay Buddhists sometimes say a short meal reflection before eating.

games.q: what does “few supports for life” mean?
o: the friends who stand by you when you're sick
life rests on a few things that can also fail
a call to live with as little as possible

games.q: two views, one meeting point — tap the pairs.
p: the body cared for, then awakening
hold the body like something borrowed
use it wisely, so practice goes on

s: Buddhism teaches that caring for the body doesn't matter
in the traditional story, the Buddha ate Sujata's milk-rice and then awoke; the body is the boat.
Nagarjuna wrote that even the supports of life can become causes of death
in the Precious Garland: the causes of death are many, the supports few, and even those can turn.
if medicine can harm, the wise move is to avoid it
the monks' reflection uses medicine wisely, to ease sickness, without clinging to the body.

games.q: your friend says the 'don't cling to the body' view is just an excuse to skip the gym and eat junk. what's that view's strongest case?
o: the body doesn't matter at all, so nothing you do to it counts.
supports fail sooner or later; peace that hangs only on them breaks.
Nagarjuna said the body is a boat you should never rest in.
games.why: not neglect: non-clinging. both views meet in the monks' reflection: use food and medicine wisely, care fully, cling not at all.

practice: If there's water near you, take one slow sip and feel it all the way down: one of the few supports, arriving. If there isn't, take one full breath the same way.
Then sit with the body that sip or breath just cared for, without needing it to last forever.

wordCard.voice: Few supports for life: food, medicine, shelter, warmth. Few, and fallible. Tend them wisely, without clinging.

orig.note: Pali: medicine, one of the few supports a monk may use, with reflection.

carryVoice: Here's the line: few supports, tended well and held lightly, like something borrowed. Day sixteen thirty-four, cared for.

sources.ref: Nagarjuna, Ratnavali (Precious Garland): the causes of death are many, those of life few, and even these can become causes of death
Majjhima Nikaya 2 (Sabbasava Sutta: the wise reflection on using almsfood and medicine)
traditional life story of the Buddha (Nidanakatha): Sujata's offering of milk-rice before the awakening
